h: A fortune tied up in a famous will
p: The story of Brodsworth starts with one of the strangest wills in English history. Peter Thellusson, a wealthy banker who died in 1797, left his fortune to build up for generations rather than go to his children and grandchildren. The legal arguments dragged on for decades, Parliament even passed a law to stop anyone doing the same again, and the case is often said to have inspired the endless lawsuit in Dickens's Bleak House.

When the money was finally released, Charles Sabine Augustus Thellusson used his share to build Brodsworth in the 1860s, filling it with the latest comforts and Italian marble sculpture. The house stayed in the family until the last of them, Sylvia Grant-Dalton, died in 1988. English Heritage took it on soon after and chose to conserve it as found rather than restore it to shiny perfection.
Look out for the marble statues dotted around the gardens, which fit right in with the grand Victorian taste of the house.
Give yourself around three hours to do the house and gardens justice, more if the kids get stuck into the play area.

Doncaster has a few more gems close by. Conisbrough Castle, with its striking round keep, is a short drive away and is also looked after by English Heritage. Cusworth Hall, a Georgian house set in parkland on the edge of town, makes a nice free-roaming walk, and the Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Branton is a big hit with families. Racing fans will know Doncaster as home of the St Leger, one of the oldest classic races in the calendar, and the Danum Gallery, Library and Museum in the town centre is a good stop for local history.
